analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal ban on exporting American crude oil.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in House committees until the Congress ended in January 2017, even though Congress separately lifted the oil export ban in late 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 1970s, federal law has generally banned exporting crude oil produced in the United States, keeping the oil available to domestic refiners. This bill would wipe out that restriction entirely and bar any federal official from limiting crude oil exports, while ordering a study of the right size for the government's emergency oil stockpile. Its main effect would be to let oil producers sell their crude on the world market at world prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Crude oil producers and exporters gain the most, because they could sell American crude at higher world-market prices instead of the discounted prices domestic refiners paid under the ban.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 103 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, the law that has restricted energy exports since the 1970s, and prohibits any federal official from imposing or enforcing any restriction on crude oil exports [S3].

Its stated findings argue that removal of export restrictions will provide domestic economic benefits and enhanced energy security, and the bill orders the Energy Secretary to recommend the appropriate size and purpose of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve within 120 days of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Domestic refiners, who had benefited from buying crude at discounted prices under the export ban, would lose that advantage; consumers could face somewhat higher crude-linked costs depending on market conditions, though studies of the actual 2015 repeal found the gasoline price effect was small.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the export ban ends a policy tool that kept American crude oil at home, which during a supply emergency could mean less oil available to domestic refiners; the bill only orders a study of the emergency stockpile rather than guaranteeing any replacement protection [S2].

Exporting crude at world prices raises the price domestic refiners pay for crude, a cost that can pass through to prices at the pump, which is why the refining industry opposed lifting the ban; the bill contains no consumer-price safeguards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward win for oil producers: it removes a 1970s-era restriction so crude can be sold at world prices. Independent analyses of the policy as actually adopted found small price effects on consumers, but the bill offers nothing to consumers in exchange, and it deliberately strips future administrations of any authority to restrict exports even in an emergency. A modest SPR study is the only offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, never received a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 3, 2015 by Rep. Joe Barton of Texas with 12 Republican cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs committees [S5] [S4].
Six days later it was referred to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on the bill for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The crude oil industry lost nothing here, because Congress went ahead and lifted the export ban anyway in the December 2015 omnibus spending law, meaning the industry got what this bill sought without this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The crude oil industry, via other legislation

for.name: Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the crude oil export ban

sides.party_line_note: All 13 members who backed the bill, the sponsor and 12 cosponsors, were Republicans; no Democrat was listed as a supporter and no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would let producers sell American crude at higher world-market prices instead of the discounted domestic prices the export ban created. Any cost lands on refiners and potentially consumers at the pump, with no safeguard in the bill.

Refiners had enjoyed buying domestic crude at a discount because it could not be exported; lifting the ban raises their input costs. In this case the refiners' interest ran alongside consumers' interest in keeping crude at home.

Access to export markets would support more drilling activity, boosting demand for oilfield services. The benefit depends on world oil prices, which fell sharply in 2015, blunting the practical effect.
